newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition to boycott parliament.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition to boycott parliament.

text.p: The Serbian opposition planned to boycott Tuesday's session of Federal Parliament after more than three weeks of protests failed to force President Slobodan Milosevic to accept its victories in annulled local elections.

Zoran Djindjic, one of the leaders of the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) on Monday told independent radio B-92 there was no point in sitting in the assembly which diplomats regard as a rubber-stamp for Milosevic's decisions.
As Djindjic threatened the walk-out, tens of thousands of protesters continued their daily pro-democracy demonstrations into their fourth week.
Monday's crowd of some 100,000 filled the city centre to renew demands that Milosevic back down on a decision to overturn opposition victories in local elections last month.
Earlier more than 40,000 students also rallied, this time venting their anger at police headqarters over the alleged beating of an opposition supporter.

The students were outraged by reports of a savage beating meted out in prison to Dejan Bulatovic, 21, a worker from the northeastern town of Sid who was arrested on Friday for carrying an effigy of Milosevic in prison garb.

Radio B-92 said Bulatovic was sentenced to 25 days in prison for disturbing public law and order. He was one of about 100 protesters that the opposition alleged had been detained for participating in the marches.
The United States notched up pressure on Milosevic to talk to the opposition by cancelling a meeting between the Serbian president and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum.
A U.S. official said Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum had been scheduled to meet Milosevic in Belgrade later this week after a NATO meeting but decided to call it off.

"We're cutting him (Milosevic) off little by little," said the official, adding: "He's doing it because he doesn't think it's useful to talk to Milosevic at this particular moment...It's in reaction to recent events, absolutely."
Kornblum's boss, Secretary of State Warren Christopher underlined the message, issuing a stern warning for Milosevic not to use violence to put down the protests.
"I would hope and expect that there would be a unified action on the part of NATO members reflecting the comments that I've just made," he told a news conference in Brussels.
Christopher did not say what action he expected but appeared to be referring to a joint statement or proposal.
The daily round of protests in Belgrade are the most sustained challenge to Milosevic's nine years of rule in which he has maintained a tight grip over state institutions.
Despite the rallies that seem to grow with each day and the barrage of U.S.-led international criticism, Milosevic maintained an aloof image of stability and control.
He dominated the first ten minutes of the state-controlled national television news bulletin, with plans to upgrade a trans-national highway system.
The demonstrations rated a passing mention of "fewer opposition supporters than before who walked around Belgrade city, disrupting traffic."
Milosevic's powerful wife Mira Markovic, who also leads the United Yugoslav Left (JUL) in coaltion with the ruling Socialists, also appeared in an attack on Zajedno's rallies.
"JUL condemns the activity of the coalition Zajedno, reflected in street demonstrations along with violence, terrorism and jepoardising the safety of Belgraders," she said.
"The consequence of such protests is material damage, destruction of the countries image, and disruption of the production process."

Apart from two days of protests in which marchers smashed windows in state television and newspaper offices, Zajedno organisers have kept strict control over the rallies, limiting attacks to shouted insults and building damage to egg-stains.
The police have kept a low profile but Zajedno officials are concerned that Milosevic might yet run out of patience and use force to snuff out the protests.
